newsitem.title: TURKEY: Stalled Turkish cotton futures may begin this year.
newsitem.headline: Stalled Turkish cotton futures may begin this year.

text.p: Turkey's first commodities futures market, initially due to trade cotton contracts, is being readied for opening by the end of 1997 after years of stalemate over its control by two government institutions.

Burak Ar, coordinator of the Izmir Futures Mercantile Exchange (IZVIP), said a major legal hurdle was overcome last week when the industry ministry published an act on the establishment of futures commodities exchanges.
"We are now trying to open the market by the end of this year," he told Reuters.
"We will soon install the software, which is being prepared by a local company, and later exchange membership will start."

The opening of the exchange, masterminded by the Izmir Trade Bourse (ITB) as early as 1991, has been hampered due to a row between the ITB and Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) over the control of contract transactions.
The SPK says it is the sole authority to establish futures exchanges and should control futures contracts because they are securities.

But the industry ministry act, which took effect on August 6, said local trade bourses could establish such exchanges after getting permission from the ministry, effectively ending the row between the SPK and ITB.
IZVIP will begin accepting members soon, Ar said. The total number of members would be 50, including six foreign companies.
"After the members are in place, the training of the brokers and local traders on the premises will be started," he said.
The SPK will be part of the transactions inspection board, according to the act.
The contracts to be used in the market can be denominated in Turkish lira or foreign currencies.

Ar said the design of the futures contracts was completed with help from the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT), which has also indicated that it will cooperate in future with IZVIP on use of the transactions software.
He said the cotton to be traded on the market would face "meticulous" inspection by the exchange's quality-control units, which are already in place.
The exchange is aimed at attracting standard cotton from all over Turkey and from nearby producers such as Uzbekistan and Greece.
Local cotton producers and textile industrialists have repeatedly said the exchange will help boost Turkey's cotton and textiles production and prevent price and output fluctuations.
